column2: On the authority of al-Miqdām ibn Maʿdīkarib, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say:

“The son of Ādam fills no vessel worse than his stomach. It is enough for the son of Ādam to have a few morsels to keep his back upright. But if he must, then a third for his food, a third for his drink and a third for his breath.” Reported by Imam Aḥmad, al-Tirmidhī, al-Nasāʾī and Ibn Mājah; al-Tirmidhī said: A ḥasan hadith.
“It is enough for the son of Ādam”: it suffices him to keep himself alive and maintain his strength.
Luqaymāt (“a few morsels”): plural of luqaymah, the diminutive of luqmah (a mouthful).
“To keep his back (ṣulbahu) upright”: his spine, so that he has the strength for obedience.
“But if he must”: go beyond what was mentioned, then let it be in thirds:
“a third for his food”: what he eats, he gives it [a third];
“and a third for his drink”: what he drinks, he gives it [a third];
“and a third for his breath (nafas)”: with the fāʾ vowelled; he leaves it so that he can breathe, and gains a certain clarity and refinement.
The printed text reads لقيمان, evidently for لقيمات (“a few morsels”), the form glossed in the vocabulary.

Not indulging in food and drink. This is a comprehensive principle containing all the principles of medicine; if people applied it, the pharmacists' shops would stand idle, for the root of every disease is overeating. This is some of the benefit of eating little and not filling oneself with food for the health of the body.

As for its benefits for the heart, it brings tenderness of heart, strength of understanding, humility of soul and weakening of desire and anger—unlike indulging in food and drink, which weighs down the body, dulls the wits, brings on sleep and weakens one for worship.
